title: Service Communication and Cascading Failure

sections.title: How a Failure Crosses Service Boundaries
Verifying Behavior During Slowdown and Recovery

html:
Service Communication and Cascading Failure

An uncertain result is one consequence of a slow dependency. Another appears before the caller reaches its deadline: the application may run out of workers while requests wait for the remote response. Baodium encountered this failure after adding an external fraud-scoring provider to checkout.

To improve fraud detection during checkout, Baodium’s engineers integrated an external fraud-scoring provider. Order Service called Fraud Service, which prepared the assessment inputs, contacted the provider, and returned an approval, denial, or decision requiring human review. Payment could begin only after an acceptable risk decision.

Before release, the engineers checked that the provider returned the expected decisions. Its calls averaged about 80 milliseconds, and checkout finished within its deadline. The integration went into production.

Six weeks later, the mean provider-call duration increased to nearly two seconds. The provider continued returning valid decisions, but checkout requests began queuing; Order Service ran out of available workers even though CPU utilization was low.

The investigation began by identifying which workers and outbound calls remained assigned during the wait. The team then had to choose admission limits, an end-to-end deadline, and a customer-visible outcome for assessments that could not finish during the synchronous request.

How a Failure Crosses Service Boundaries

Order Service assigned a worker to checkout, validated the cart, and called Fraud Service. Fraud Service acquired a slot in its provider client and sent the assessment. The Order Service worker then waited for Fraud Service, while Fraud Service waited for the provider. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch04-nested}\) shows the nesting.

The affected Order Service used blocking workers. A worker waiting for network I/O consumed little CPU, but could not process another checkout. As provider calls took longer, more incoming checkouts found workers already assigned to earlier requests.

Fraud Service had its own limit on active provider requests; once those slots were assigned, subsequent assessments queued before contacting the provider. Their Order Service callers waited through that queue as well.

During the incident, one checkout occupied resources in several services, and each synchronous caller included downstream waiting in its response duration.

The capacity calculation from Chapter 2 confirmed the diagnosis. At one Order Service instance, 200 checkouts per second spent at least 2.05 seconds in the fraud-dependent interval, including processing around the provider call. Sustaining that rate would require 410 workers for that interval alone, against a configured pool of 300. Requests therefore queued or failed instead of completing at the offered rate.

An asynchronous runtime would change the resource accounting. A coroutine could release its thread while awaiting network I/O, but the request would still use memory and could occupy a stream, client connection, or admission slot. The same investigation applies, using the resources allocated by that implementation.

Diagnosis Before Configuration Changes

Order Service’s worker pool was full, so the first proposal was to add workers. Before making it, we need to establish what those workers are doing. If they are waiting on Fraud Service, more workers do not increase what the provider receives, because Fraud Service’s own admission limit already caps concurrent provider calls. They increase the number of checkouts admitted into the wait, each holding a worker and its share of memory, so the queue grows deeper and the incident spreads further back toward the customer.

A trace of a delayed checkout shows that most of its time was spent in the Fraud Service call. Inside Fraud Service, separate measurements show time spent acquiring a provider client slot and time spent waiting after the request was sent. If acquisition time increases while provider-call duration matches its previous distribution, we investigate local client contention, additional callers, or changes in request volume. If provider-call duration increases first and acquisition delay follows, longer calls are occupying the client slots. Baodium observed the second sequence, in which longer provider calls were holding the client slots; additional Order Service workers would only have lengthened the queue in front of them.

The next design question is therefore what checkout should do once waiting for fraud evaluation would interfere with its other work.

Required Results and Deferred Work

A confirmed purchase required an acceptable fraud decision, payment authorization, inventory reservation, and a committed order record. The original handler also waited for Notification Service to send the confirmation email. These calls did not all need the same treatment.

The calls differed in their effect on checkout correctness. Without an acceptable fraud decision and an authorization, Checkout could not confirm the purchase. After the order committed, a delayed confirmation email did not undo it.

If email delivery failed after the order was committed, the purchase still existed. Returning a generic checkout error at that point could encourage the customer to submit another purchase. The application needed to return the confirmed order and complete notification separately.

Fraud evaluation had a different business requirement, because payment could not begin without an acceptable decision. A missing response therefore required a pending or unavailable result, according to the checkout policy.

Before choosing a timeout or adding a queue, we need to establish these permitted outcomes.

The result required from each checkout dependency.
Dependency Required result Incomplete outcome
Fraud Acceptable decision before payment. Defer assessment without starting payment.
Payment Confirmed authorization before proceeding. Reconcile an uncertain authorization.
Inventory Confirmed reservation before order confirmation. Resolve uncertainty or compensate a definitive rejection.
Notification Delivery after order confirmation. Retry delivery from durable work.

Baodium recorded an OrderConfirmed outbox event in the order transaction. Notification processing followed that commit, using the publication and deduplication procedure from Chapter 3. A notification outage could delay email without extending the checkout request.

We can also use these dependencies to decide which calls may execute concurrently. Independent product-page reads may be issued together. Starting payment while fraud evaluation is unresolved would violate this checkout policy, even if doing so reduced response time.

Parallel execution also needs a completion rule. If two independent calls run concurrently, the caller must decide whether it requires both results, can return a partial result, or should cancel unfinished work after one fails. That decision belongs to the operation’s contract.

Admission Before the Outbound Call

An outbound-call limit bounds the requests waiting for one dependency. Choose it against the caller resources those waits occupy and the allocation available at the receiver.

Once a slow fraud result could lead to a deferred assessment, checkout could limit how many requests waited for it. Order Service received an allocation of 80 concurrent outbound fraud calls per instance. A handler attempted to acquire a permit before sending the call. If all permits were assigned, it recorded a pending assessment and returned the checkout reference.

Acquiring a permit1 increments the number of admitted calls, and releasing it decrements that number. The check and increment must be atomic, or simultaneous handlers all observe the same available slot and admit together. A dependency-specific allocation of this kind is commonly called a bulkhead. It prevents calls to one dependency from occupying every worker available to the caller.

For instance, suppose Fraud Service accepts network connections but stops processing requests. A limit inside Fraud Service cannot prevent Order Service handlers from waiting before they reach that limit. Order Service therefore needs admission before its own outbound call.

Fraud Service separately limits the evaluations it accepts from all callers; in this configuration, it admitted at most 80 logical evaluations per instance. One evaluation used a permit across its provider attempts and retry delays. The provider client did not add another request queue behind that admission point.

Queueing and Rejection

A queue can be useful when a brief burst will finish before the waiting requests lose their value. It needs a maximum size and a maximum waiting period, both consistent with the caller’s deadline.

For this fraud path, Baodium chose immediate admission or deferral. Waiting in another local queue would use the customer deadline without producing a risk decision. Durable deferred processing was already available for work that could not begin promptly.

This choice changes what the customer receives; some checkouts that previously waited until timeout receive a pending result earlier. The application must then complete or expire those assessments under its recovery policy.

Recording a pending result uses the database and a handler. The fraud bulkhead bounds outbound waiting; ingress admission and database capacity bound the arrival rate Order Service can accept.

Choosing the Allocation

The value 80 is specific to this workload, and selecting it requires checking both the caller and the provider. Please do not copy the number. What transfers to your own system is the method of writing down how many calls the caller can afford, how many the provider can accept, and then choosing the smaller.

At the caller, tests establish how many fraud calls can coexist with other request processing without unacceptable queueing. At the provider boundary, the combined allocation must fit the account’s concurrency and request-rate allowances.

A rate limit and a concurrency limit measure different things. A provider can receive many short calls per second while few are active simultaneously. When calls take longer, the same arrival rate creates more active requests. An integration may therefore need both controls.

Per-instance limits also add together. Additional replicas, deployment overlap, other applications, and background recovery workers all contribute to the provider’s total demand. A local configuration cannot be evaluated without that wider allocation.

Chapter 9 examines these controls in more detail. For this chapter, the important placement is admission before the outbound wait, with an explicit result for work that cannot be admitted.

::: decision

**Where does the extra second come from?**

Checkout has a one-second budget for fraud evaluation. Order Service admits at most 80 concurrent fraud calls per instance. The provider has slowed: evaluations that used to return in 200 ms now take 1.2 seconds, so nearly every call exhausts the budget and the handler gives up. Your on-call engineer proposes raising the fraud deadline to three seconds so that evaluations can complete.

**Raise the deadline to three seconds. The provider is slow, not broken, and the results are still arriving.**

**Keep the one-second deadline and defer the evaluation, returning a pending checkout.**

**Keep the deadline and raise the admission limit from 80 to 240, so more evaluations can be in flight at once.**

—

A allows the measured 1.2-second evaluations to finish. If each call occupies a slot for 1.2 seconds, 80 slots support about \(80/1.2 \approx 67\) completions per second before other overhead. The three-second timeout is a cap, not the mean duration. If calls later occupy slots for the full three seconds, that estimate falls to about 27 per second. Compare both cases with arrivals and the full checkout deadline before changing the cap.

C permits more waiting calls but provides no evidence that the provider can complete more evaluations. At a given arrival rate it may increase concurrency without improving completion throughput, and it also allows more caller memory and worker slots to be occupied.

B preserves the one-second response allowance and records unfinished evaluation as durable work. The customer receives a pending checkout reference. Recovery needs its own admission limit, status endpoint, and rule preventing payment before an acceptable fraud decision. A local timeout must not cause recovery to duplicate remote work that is still executing.

The chapter uses B to preserve the response contract. A can be reasonable if the product accepts the longer response and tests establish adequate completion capacity. The choice depends on those two requirements.

:::

Deadlines for the Whole Call

The next decision is how long an admitted checkout can wait for fraud evaluation. Baodium selected a one-second maximum for the complete Fraud Service call and checked it against the rest of checkout. The allowance includes transit, local processing, provider attempts, retry delays, and the return response. The provider therefore receives less than the full one-second budget (Figure \(\ref{fig:ch04-deadline}\)).

To choose such an allowance, we begin with the customer response requirement and examine representative checkout traces. Payment, inventory, local commits, and response construction still need time after fraud approval. The proposed allocation is then tested with slow dependencies and realistic request variation.

Adding individual p99 durations will not give the checkout p99. End-to-end measurements are needed because slow intervals do not necessarily occur in the same requests. The caller also checks the time available when fraud evaluation is about to begin. If earlier work has already consumed most of the request budget, it shortens the fraud allowance or defers before sending.

Deadlines and Attempt Timeouts

A deadline applies to the complete operation; an attempt timeout applies to one call made during that operation. The two are easy to confuse, and confusing them is how a request with a one-second budget ends up spending three seconds across three patient attempts.

Suppose an assessment has one second available, and the first provider attempt uses half of it. A retry delay and the next attempt must fit the time left, with an allowance for recording and returning the result. The second attempt cannot receive a fresh one-second timeout.

Connection acquisition follows the same rule. Waiting for a stream or connection consumes the operation budget before the provider request is sent.

Client settings deserve inspection here. A read timeout may limit an individual read or a period without data, rather than the entire response. Name resolution, connection establishment, and TLS negotiation may have separate settings, so the integration needs an overall limit covering the complete local attempt.

This can be tested without depending on a production outage; a stub can delay connection establishment, response headers, or response-body delivery. Each case should finish under the intended overall deadline, subject to the measured cleanup interval.

Deadlines Between Services

Order Service passes the available fraud budget to Fraud Service, which applies it when starting provider work. Each hop accounts for elapsed time instead of assigning its default allowance again. The transport representation must support that accounting. Monotonic timestamps are suitable for elapsed time inside a process but cannot be interpreted using another host’s clock. Services need transport-supported deadlines or an agreed representation with defined treatment of elapsed time and clock differences.

The practical verification is to delay a request before provider work begins. The provider attempt must receive less time; if it receives the original allowance, the implementation has extended the caller’s deadline.

Cancellation and Continuing Work

A caller timing out and its underlying work stopping are separate events. After the caller times out, remote work may continue using a connection or provider slot. Cancellation and resource cleanup need their own mechanisms and measurements.

Consider a handler that starts a provider call in a background task and waits for it with a timeout. When the wait expires, the handler can return while the task continues using an HTTP client slot. If the handler releases its admission permit immediately, another request can begin alongside that task.

After repeated timeouts, active client work can surpass the intended admission limit. Baodium required resource ownership to continue through local call cleanup. A permit associated with active client work was released when that work finished or local cancellation completed. A library that returns earlier needs separate accounting for tasks still using resources.

Cancellation also needs to reach retry delays and nested calls. A handler sleeping before another attempt must stop when its request is canceled, unless it has deliberately transferred the work to durable recovery.

Remote execution requires separate verification. Closing the local connection does not confirm that the provider stopped processing the request. The client can release its socket while the provider continues an assessment.

For payment and inventory writes, the operation identity and reconciliation rules from Chapter 3 still apply. For resource planning, request-rate and retry limits also matter because locally completed attempts may leave work executing remotely.

A cancellation test therefore checks local resource release and, where the provider exposes the information, remote continuation. Measuring only how soon the wrapper returns misses the first problem.

Retry Eligibility and Ownership

Retries multiply when retry policies are enabled at more than one layer. Baodium assigned provider retries to Fraud Service because it had the assessment identity, provider contract, and remaining operation deadline. The gateway, service mesh, and provider SDK had retries disabled for that route.

Before any of this becomes code, the handler’s possible outcomes need to be separated, because they demand different responses and only some of them are safe to retry. A connection failure known to occur before submission may permit another attempt. A completed approval, denial, or manual-review decision ends the assessment. A timeout after submission may require lookup or repetition under the provider’s idempotency contract, because the earlier request could still be processing.

The timeout value also affects whether retrying is useful. If provider calls consistently take two seconds, repeated half-second attempts are unlikely to obtain a decision. When abandoned requests continue remotely, they can increase provider work as well.

For eligible transient failures, Fraud Service used a bounded delay with jitter, and it checked the time available before waiting and again before sending. The per-assessment attempt maximum and aggregate retry allowance both applied.

The aggregate allowance prevented every failing assessment from using its full retry policy during an outage. Once it was consumed, further assessments were deferred. A circuit breaker can additionally suspend attempts after recent calls indicate a provider problem, then permit limited probes before reopening normal access. For this incident, returned error codes alone would have been insufficient because the provider was answering slowly. Timeout or duration evidence was needed too.

The admission limit applies throughout that process, including while the breaker collects evidence. We will develop breaker sampling and retry budgets in Chapter 9.

Checkout Integration

We can now connect these decisions to the handler that chooses whether checkout proceeds or waits for recovery. Focus on the caller’s side of the boundary in the code below: the order in which it writes state, calls the provider, and records the result. The repository and client methods are stand-ins for whatever your own data layer provides, and their contracts enforce the guarded state transitions and durable operation identity from Chapter 3. The names matter less than the sequence.

[
  language=Python,
  caption={Admission and deadline handling before fraud evaluation.}]
def resolve_checkout_risk(request, checkout):
    assessment = risk_repo.get_or_create(
        checkout_id=checkout.id,
        input_version=checkout.risk_input_version,
    )

    if assessment.has_recorded_result:
        return assessment.result

    deadline = request.child_deadline(
        maximum_ms=1000,
        reserve_ms=checkout_policy.after_risk_budget_ms,
    )
    if not deadline.can_start_call():
        return risk_repo.defer_if_unresolved(
            assessment.id,
            reason="insufficient_request_time",
        )

    permit = outbound_fraud_slots.try_acquire()
    if permit is None:
        return risk_repo.defer_if_unresolved(
            assessment.id,
            reason="fraud_capacity_unavailable",
        )

    with permit:
        try:
            decision = fraud_client.evaluate(
                assessment_id=assessment.id,
                inputs=assessment.inputs,
                deadline=deadline,
                cancellation=request.cancellation,
            )
        except FraudCallUnavailable as error:
            return risk_repo.defer_if_unresolved(
                assessment.id,
                reason=error.reason,
            )

    return risk_repo.record_decision_if_current(
        assessment_id=assessment.id,
        input_version=assessment.input_version,
        decision=decision,
    )

Two failure windows need attention: a process can stop after the remote call, and concurrent handlers can submit the same assessment. The assessment record is written before the remote call so a later worker can investigate it if the process stops after dispatch. Recording only the response leaves a failure window: the provider may complete the action while the local database has no operation record. Recovery then depends on another way to locate and verify the provider’s result.

A unique database constraint prevents concurrent handlers from creating two assessments for one checkout. A separate application read followed by an insert would allow both handlers to observe absence. On a uniqueness conflict, the handler retrieves the existing assessment:

[
  language=SQL,
  caption={A unique constraint makes the second concurrent submission
           retrieve the first assessment instead of creating another.}]
CREATE TABLE risk_assessments (
    id            UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    checkout_id   UUID NOT NULL,
    input_version INT  NOT NULL,
    state         TEXT NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT one_per_checkout UNIQUE (checkout_id)
);

-- Whichever handler arrives second inserts nothing and reads
-- the row the first one created.
INSERT INTO risk_assessments
    (id, checkout_id, input_version, state)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, 'RISK_EVALUATION_PENDING')
ON CONFLICT (checkout_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;

If the insert returns no row, the handler selects the existing assessment by checkout_id and proceeds with that one. Both submissions then refer to the same assessment, and the provider receives one evaluation request. The alternative, taking a lock on the checkout row for the duration, also works and is sometimes simpler to reason about, but it holds a database resource across the decision and Chapter 7 explains why that gets expensive under load.

The deferred update is conditional. If another handler has already recorded approval, a late timeout must not replace it with pending state. The method retrieves the recorded outcome when the assessment has already been resolved.

The decision update also checks whether the assessment still applies to the current checkout inputs. A canceled checkout or changed cart must not proceed to payment because an earlier assessment returned approval.

The outbound client has no independent retry policy; Fraud Service owns permitted provider retries and receives the inherited deadline. The client rechecks available time before sending and completes local cleanup before the permit is released.

Caller cancellation may interrupt the handler before it records a deferred result. Background recovery can still find the unfinished assessment created before the call. This avoids relying on an exception handler as the only place where recovery is scheduled.

Deferred Checkout and Customer Expectations

Sometimes the truthful answer to a customer is that the purchase has been accepted but is not finished, and the interface has to have somewhere to put that.

A pending record needs a customer-facing contract. The customer should be able to determine whether the purchase was confirmed, whether payment began, and where to obtain an update.

For deferred fraud evaluation, Baodium returned the checkout reference and explained that verification was pending and payment had not started. The status endpoint read the stored checkout state and did not submit another evaluation when that state was unresolved. Repeated customer refreshes therefore added status reads without creating more provider calls. Recovery workers submitted those calls under a separate rate and concurrency allocation.

The application distinguished a missing provider decision from a completed decision requiring review.

Unfinished evaluation and manual review require different recovery work.
State Follow-up
RISK_EVALUATION_PENDING A worker obtains or recovers the provider decision.
RISK_MANUAL_REVIEW The risk-review process supplies the required judgment.

The recovery worker used a new execution deadline while preserving the assessment identity. It shared the provider allocation with live requests so a backlog could not consume all available access.

A delayed approval also needed revalidation before payment, because price, cart contents, delivery eligibility, and risk-relevant account data could have changed. Different assessment inputs required an explicitly linked new assessment, and a price change could require customer confirmation.

Baodium defined how long a deferred checkout could be continued and what happened when that period expired. If recovery could no longer process the backlog under that policy, accepting further deferred work would create promises the application could not fulfill. Asynchronous completion requires status retrieval, expiry, cancellation, and revalidation, alongside the worker that eventually calls the provider.

Verifying Behavior During Slowdown and Recovery

The revised path was tested with a provider stub that could return decisions, reject requests, delay responses, or never respond. This made it possible to verify the application under specific conditions instead of relying on occasional provider failures. When the stub returned valid decisions slowly, the test checked active fraud calls, deferred outcomes, and completion of unrelated requests. The load generator recorded the arrival rate it achieved so its own waiting would not reduce the intended demand.

When the stub never responded, the test checked deadlines and local resource cleanup. Active client requests and background tasks could not continue accumulating after callers returned.

The team counted attempts at the provider boundary to verify retry ownership. This detected additional attempts from infrastructure or SDK settings that an application-loop counter would miss.

Recovery was tested with a pending backlog while live checkouts continued. Workers had to process that backlog under the shared provider allocation, and canceled or expired checkouts had to stop before payment.

A release evaluation needed both technical and business outcomes, because lower response latency could result from returning pending status to more customers. Confirmed checkout rate, deferred completion time, and expiry count showed whether those customers eventually obtained a useful result.

Production Measurements

The production dashboards used the same request boundaries as the failure tests, which let the team compare the measurements directly. For example, query-execution time cannot be compared with an interval that also includes connection acquisition without separating the waits.

Order Service reported assigned workers, outbound fraud calls, and admission rejections; Fraud Service reported admitted evaluations, provider attempts, and deferred reasons. Separate acquisition and provider-call timers identified waiting for local resources and waiting after a request was sent.

The provider-call timer included network time. It could identify a slow external call, but only the provider could say how long its own processing took. For recovery, the useful measurements were pending count, oldest pending age, completion rate, and expired assessments. If the backlog continued increasing after the provider recovered, the team could examine worker capacity, provider allocation, or repeated recovery failures.

Traces connected an individual checkout to its assessment and attempts, while aggregate metrics used bounded labels such as caller, instance, and outcome. Operation identities were available in traces and investigation records.

This allowed the on-call engineer to distinguish a slow live request from a deferred assessment and a case awaiting human review. Each required a different response.

Summary

Baodium’s fraud provider continued returning valid decisions after its average response time rose toward two seconds. The incident came from the time Order Service workers spent waiting. A growing set of unfinished requests occupied the worker allocation, and new checkouts queued even though CPU utilization remained low.

The revised checkout contract specifies which decisions must precede payment and what the customer receives if the assessment cannot finish synchronously. Admission limits waiting before the outbound call. One deadline covers the full operation, and one component owns retry decisions so that timeouts at several layers do not multiply attempts. Cancellation is treated as a local signal until the team has verified what the remote provider does with an interrupted call. A durable pending assessment preserves the state required to finish the purchase later.

These controls must be tested together under provider slowdown and recovery. A timeout without bounded admission still permits a large number of simultaneous waits; a retry policy without durable identity can repeat an action; and a pending response without recovery ownership leaves the customer waiting indefinitely. Chapter 5 addresses a different way to reduce dependency demand: reusing a result when the application’s freshness requirements permit it.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & Checkout may defer fraud evaluation without beginning payment, provided the customer receives a durable reference and the assessment is completed or expired under a defined policy.
Condition that tests it & A dependency slows while callers continue admitting requests or retries.
Constraint or invariant & Order Service limits outbound fraud calls before sending. Fraud Service separately limits evaluations and provider requests. Live processing and recovery share the provider allocation.
Evidence and uncertainty & Provider-call duration increased from about 80 milliseconds to nearly two seconds. Client-acquisition delay followed, and Order Service exhausted its available workers. Verification measures both bounded waiting and eventual checkout outcomes.

Whether provider work continues after local cancellation, and whether deferred assessments can be completed under the recovery policy during an extended slowdown.
Signal and evaluation window & During the slowdown test, measure queue duration, occupied workers, and downstream attempts against the shared deadline.
Control and decision & Bound synchronous waiting and record unfinished assessments. Proceed to payment only after an acceptable risk decision, with current checkout data and a permitted state transition.
Owner and review trigger & The checkout owner defines customer outcomes and expiry. The Fraud Service owner manages provider admission, retry eligibility, and assessment recovery. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.
:::

  1. A permit is one unit of a concurrency limiter: acquiring it increments the number of admitted calls, and releasing it decrements that number.↩︎
